newsitem.title: USA: Portrait of Evita under spotlight in Miami museum.
newsitem.headline: Portrait of Evita under spotlight in Miami museum.

text.p: When a Florida museum displayed what it claimed to be the only known life portrait of Eva Peron, many people questioned whether this was true.
After all, Eva Peron was one of the most iconographed figures of the 20th century. Portraits of her can still be found hanging in shops and homes throughout Argentina.

Now the museum may have another problem. Aside from proving this is the only real life portrait of Argentina's former First Lady, there is also doubt over whether the woman in their picture is even Eva Peron at all.
In a life portrait, the subject actually poses for the artist and is not copied from memory or a photograph.

The son of Brazilian master Candido Portinari (1903-1962), who is the artist responsible for the painting, has written to the Museum of Arts and Science in Daytona Beach and said he knew of only 16 women painted by his father in the 1940s.
None of them was 21-year-old Evita Duarte, who later married Juan Peron, future president of Argentina.
"One of them looks like yours, but it is a portrait of Eva Rubinstein," daughter of the late piansit Artur Rubinstein, Joao Portinari wrote.
Another opinion comes from Vivian Pieffer, Miami director of the esteemed auction house Christies.
"I've only seen a slide, not the actual portrait, but it appears to be a painting auctioned in New York in 1987," she said on Thursday.
"It's an absolutely beautiful portrait, but I don't think it's Eva Peron."
Pieffer thinks the young woman is Cecila Barbosa, daughter-in-law of a former Brazilian president and wife of the late Brazilian diplomat Ruy Barbosa.
Museum director Gary Libby has not returned phone calls seeking comment on the issue.

In an interview before the portrait's Jan. 7 debut, he said it came from the collection of the late Florida real estate magnate Anderson Bouchelle, who bought it from a Peronista family who fled Argentina and settled in Miami.
Libby said the portrait was painted in 1940, four years before the young Eva Duarte met her future husband.
She was a star on Argentine radio at the time and theatrical agent Eduardo Ginely commissioned Portinari to paint her, Libby said.

None of its owners publicly exhibited the painting until the museum gave it a highly publicised debut. Libby said his own research showed no other life portrait has ever been catalogued or publicly shown of Evita.
Museum spokeswoman Cathy Lea declined to answer questions about the controversy but issued a statement saying notes on the back of the painting identify it as "Eva Duarte".
The statement described the controversy as one "that Evita would have loved".
